extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, USPTO policymakers, patent practitioners, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and applying quantitative metrics to evaluate patent examiner behavior, productivity, consistency, and their effects on patent quality and USPTO backlog. The page proposes new ratios and discusses how to interpret them across examiners, workgroups, and technology centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance rate was defined as the total number of granted patents by the specific examiner divided by the total number of years that examiner had been at the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the author's first study to measure examiner propensity to grant; captures differences between primary and secondary examiners. However, the metric 'suffers from a denominator problem' because it does not account for the total number of applications on an examiner's docket, abandons, or pending prosecution. Practitioners should be aware that allowance rate alone can be misleading (e.g., artificially high because of many pending cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Actions per Grant Ratio (OGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: OGR = total number of Office Actions written by that examiner divided by the total number of grants. It 'reflects the average number of office actions it takes before an examiner grants a patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures examiner behavior regarding how many interactions occur before allowance; indirectly accounts for abandonments because Office Actions are written regardless of whether an application is later abandoned or granted. To calculate: isolate active examiners (with pending applications), count every Office Action ever written by that examiner, determine how many patents the examiner has allowed, and divide Office Actions by grants. Interpretations: most examiners have OGR under 4.0 (≈ one grant per four Office Actions); high OGRs concentrate in certain Technology Centers (e.g., 1600/1700/3600). Use OGR to determine how frequently an examiner grants a patent and to identify examiners who write many Office Actions without granting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Actions per Disposal Ratio (ODR)
rubrics_metrics.description: ODR = Office Actions / (grants + abandonments). This measures how many Office Actions an examiner writes on average before a 'disposal' (either allowance or abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ODR hints at how long it may take for an applicant to receive a patent or abandon the application and helps inform practitioner decisions (e.g., whether to file a continuation, appeal, or abandon). Most examiners have ODR less than 3.0 (≈ a disposal every three Office Actions). Use ODR to assess speed-to-resolution independent of grants alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant to Examiner Ratio (GER)
rubrics_metrics.description: GER determines what proportion of patents a cohort of examiners grants relative to that cohort's share of total examiners. Calculated as the percentage of patents issued by a cohort divided by the percentage of examiners in that cohort (cohorts defined by OGR segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If GER = 1, the cohort issues patents in proportion to its share of examiners. GER > 1 means the cohort issues more patents than its proportional share (contributing to reducing backlog); GER < 1 means issuing fewer. Example interpretation: examiners with OGR 0.01–3.00 have GER > 1 (they help reduce backlog), whereas examiners with OGR > 3.00 have GER < 1 (they do not contribute to removing backlog and may increase it). GER is agnostic to substantive application quality or technology differences and should be used with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs. Secondary examiner status
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary examiners are senior (at least five years' experience) with full signatory authority; secondary examiners are junior (< five years), supervised, and lack signatory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classification is an important evaluative dimension: secondary examiners tend to issue patents at a much lower rate, take longer to issue patents, and default to rejection (creating low allowance rates), whereas primary examiners issue patents more quickly, default more to allowance, and account for a large share of granted patents. Evaluations should adjust for experience and signatory authority when comparing examiner behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Signatory authority allows a primary examiner to sign off on his or her own Office Actions without supervisor review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signatory authority affects speed and default behavior—primary examiners with signatory authority often have higher allowance rates and shorter prosecution times. When measuring examiner productivity or consistency, account for signatory status because it changes incentives and error-scrutiny dynamics (erroneous allowances are more visible and potentially penalized, affecting behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for docket composition (denominator problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurements must account for the total number of applications on an examiner's docket and applicant abandonments; relying solely on counts like number of grants per years of service leads to a denominator problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author created OGR and ODR specifically to correct the allowance-rate denominator problem by including office actions and abandonments. Any metric aiming to reflect examiner behavior or productivity should include Office Actions, grants, and abandonments (and focus on active examiners with pending dockets) to avoid misleading conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-technology and intra-workgroup consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners' metrics (OGR, ODR, allowance rates) can vary widely across Technology Centers and even among workgroups within the same Technology Center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should be segmented by Technology Center and workgroup because differing class/subclass mixes and art-unit practices can produce divergent metric distributions (example: within TC1600, workgroup 1610 had many examiners with OGR > 10 while 1620 had many with OGR 1.01–2.00). Use segmentation to detect inconsistent application of patentability rules and to avoid misleading comparisons across heterogeneous groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting outliers for targeted review
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify examiners whose OGR (or other metrics) are several standard deviations from the mean for further scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO should survey prosecution dockets for examiners with extreme OGRs to determine which examiners 'are hurting innovation more.' Suggested follow-ups: examine individual prosecution histories, perform substantive analysis of Office Actions, and compare litigation/invalidity rates for high vs low OGR examiners. Use outlier detection as a triage to prioritize quality-control review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking examiner metrics to patent quality and litigation/invalidation outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metric-based segmentation (e.g., OGR strata) to analyze downstream outcomes such as litigation rates and invalidated patents associated with particular examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends comparing litigation and invalidation rates across examiners with different OGR/allowance profiles (as done in prior work) to determine whether high allowance rates or particular OGR patterns correlate with poor patent quality. Such substantive outcome analysis complements productivity metrics and helps balance speed/backlog reduction with patent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity vs. backlog contribution (speed and throughput metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments should consider both how quickly examiners move cases (first Office Action pendency, time-to-allowance) and how cohorts contribute to reducing the backlog (using GER and OGR interpretations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics should be interpreted jointly: low OGR and GER > 1 indicate cohorts that allow patents efficiently and help reduce backlog; high OGR and GER < 1 indicate cohorts that write many Office Actions but do not proportionally reduce the backlog. Use combined metrics (OGR, ODR, GER, first-action pendency) to balance incentives between rapid disposal and maintaining patentability standards.
